bib.title: Toward Efficient Agents: Memory, Tool learning, and Planning

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Toward Efficient Agents: A Survey of Memory, Tool Use, and Planning", Xiaofang Yang, Lijun Li, Heng Zhou, Tong Zhu et al. (Shanghai AI Lab, Fudan, others), arXiv 2601.14192 v2 (cover dated 20 Jan 2026, v2 stamp 3 Jul 2026), preprint, 2026.

COVERAGE: 217,099 of 217,099 chars extracted (all 2,687 lines). I read the abstract, the contents, sections 1-8 in full, and the references (lines 1894-2687) by skim. The PDF has no appendices; it ends with the references. Extraction was clean text after I forced UTF-8 replacement for one surrogate character.

HEADLINE FOR YOUR NOTE: this is a survey with NO original experiments. I found no benchmark tables and no cost breakdown of tokens or calls per task. A full-text search for percent and multiplier figures found one number, the CoA result below. It gives a vocabulary and a cost model for agent cost. It does not supply measured per-task costs, so do not cite it for "an agent costs X". Cite it for definitions and for the taxonomy of levers.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: The loop is Input -> [Memory(context) -> Planning(decision) -> Tool Use(action) -> Observation(feedback)]^n -> Solution. Each step's output becomes the next step's input cost, so tokens compound.
  number: none
  setup: conceptual framing in the Introduction. No measurement.
  quote: "This cycle creates a compounding accumulation of tokens, where the output of stepn becomes the input cost of stepn+1 , resulting in high inference costs and slow response times."
  where: p4-5, ~line 176
- claim: Efficient agent is defined as a system-level property, not a smaller model. It means maximising task success while minimising tokens, latency and compute across memory, tools and planning.
  number: none
  quote: "Efficient agentis not a smaller model, but as an agentic system optimized to maximize task suc-cess rates while minimizing resource consumption, including token usage, inference latency, and computational cost across memory, tool usage, and planning modules."
  where: p5, ~line 179
- claim: A cost model separates pure-LLM cost (generation only) from agent cost, which adds tool, memory and retry terms. The indicators are 0/1 flags, so the formula says whether a component is used, not how many times.
  number: none
  setup: stylised approximation (the paper's own notation), not fitted to data
  quote: "CostLLM ≈αN tok, ... Costagent ≈αN tok +I tool ·Cost tool +I mem ·Cost mem +I retry ·Cost retry, where Itool,Imem,Iretry ∈ {0, 1}are indicator variables"
  where: p6, lines 259-308. Conclusion drawn there: "improving agent efficiency is not only about reducing language generation, but also about reducing the frequency and improving the selectivity of tool or memory invocations and retries along a trajectory".
- claim: Efficiency must be judged effectiveness-first, either as quality at a fixed budget or as cost at matched quality (a Pareto view). The survey says most papers do not report this cleanly.
  number: none
  quote: "efficiency should not be evaluated in isolation. A practical evaluation protocol first establishes whether an agent or component remains effective, and then compares cost under a comparable effectiveness level, or compares effectiveness under a fixed cost budget."
  where: p39, line 1680-1685
- claim: Deep-research agents can issue very many tool calls. This is the only per-task scale figure in the paper, and it is second-hand (cites [144]).
  number: 600 search calls
  setup: a single deep-research problem, cited from another paper. The model and benchmark are not given.
  quote: "LLMs may call the search API for 600 times to resolve a deep research problem [144]."
  where: p25, line 1091
- claim: The only measured efficiency figures in the paper: CoA cuts inference time by over 30% versus Toolformer, and TinyAgent's tool classifier roughly halves the prompt.
  number: ">30% inference time (CoA vs Toolformer)"; "nearly half of the prompt size" (TinyAgent)
  setup: secondhand from CoA [29] and TinyAgent [21]. The survey gives no benchmark, model or baseline-matching detail, so I cannot say whether the baselines are compute- or call-matched.
  quote: "CoA performs better while reducing more than 30% inference time than Toolformer." / "Since only a small fraction of tool descriptions are put into the prompt, it efficiently reduces nearly half of the prompt size."
  where: p29 line 1264; p28 lines 1208-1210
- claim: The levers are grouped by where they cut cost.
  Memory:
    1. Bound the prompt by compression or rewriting (MEM1, MemAgent, AgentFold).
    2. Use latent or KV memory (Activation Beacon, MemoRAG, MemoryLLM).
    3. Select and retrieve only a few items (graph, hierarchical, query-adaptive).
    4. Update with cheap rules and reserve LLM calls for hard cases (hybrid management).
  Tools:
    5. Retrieve or classify tools rather than listing all of them.
    6. Call tools in parallel (LLMCompiler).
    7. Add tool-use penalties in RL (OTC-PO, ToolOrchestra, AutoTIR).
    8. Call a tool only when needed (SMART, A2FM, IKEA).
  Planning:
    9. Spend deliberation adaptively (SwiftSage, Ares).
    10. Prune search (CATS, ToolChain*).
    11. Decompose into plan and execution (ReWOO).
    12. Cache plans and skills (agentic plan caching, Voyager).
  Multi-agent:
    13. Sparsify the communication topology (Chain-of-Agents, AgentPrune).
    14. Distill coordination into one model (MAGDI, D&R).
  number: none (14 levers is my count)
  quote: "Across both categories, a common design principle emerges: memory writes are selectively gated so that the agent avoids redundantly re-encoding stable or low-information content." / "the unifying trend is the migration of computation from expensiveonline searchto cheaper offline learning, reusable memory, or structured retrieval."
  where: p10 line 472; p38 lines 1646-1647
- claim: Compression has a quality cost. Rule-based forgetting cuts memory size and retrieval time but costs task performance (per A-MEM), and heavier compression lowers accuracy (per LightMem).
  number: none
  quote: "Experimental results in A-MEM [185] suggest that forgetting-curve-based memory management effectively controls memory size and reduces retrieval time. However, it also leads to a substantial drop in task performance." / "excessive compression leads to poorer accuracy, whereas milder compression better preserves performance but incurs relatively higher cost."
  where: p14 lines 640-642; p24 lines 1049-1051
- claim: Maintenance is itself a cost. LLM-managed memory adds calls, and synchronous updates cost more calls and latency than async or offline ones (MemoryOS vs LightMem). Offloading does not cut total compute.
  number: none
  quote: "such real-time updates incur frequent LLM calls per response, leading to higher latency and financial costs. ... LightMem [23] adopts a hybrid architecture ... significantly reducing inference time while maintaining similar overall computational costs."
  where: p24 lines 1056-1060
- claim: Multi-agent communication cost is claimed to be quadratic by default and near-linear under chain or DAG topologies.
  number: "O(N^2) toward O(N)"
  setup: asserted, not measured here
  quote: "reducing message complexity fromO(N 2) toward O(N) through structured topologies such as chains or DAGs."
  where: p37 line 1606
- claim: Skills and plan caches are an amortisation trade-off. They pay off only if reuse exceeds the construction and retrieval cost.
  number: none
  quote: "Constructing and maintaining skills may be costly for a single task, but the cost can be justified if the learned skills are reused across many future tasks, users, or domains."
  where: p21 lines 934-936
- claim: More planning has diminishing returns, and the right unit of analysis is end-to-end cost (tokens, time, external actions, retries, coordination).
  number: none
  quote: "the right unit of analysis is end-to-end cost, including tokens, wall-clock time, external actions, retries, and coordination overhead." / "Additional search, reflection, or debate has diminishing returns"
  where: p38 lines 1652-1664
- claim: Metric families to use when reporting cost: token and dollar cost, time, resource (GPU memory), and interaction (LLM calls per response, steps, trials, nodes). Cost-of-pass [22] combines cost with success probability. TPS-Bench, CostBench, MemBench and Evo-Memory are the cost-aware benchmarks.
  number: none
  quote: "TPS-Bench [181] evaluates planning and tooling efficiency with token usage, end-to-end time, and tool-call turns, and further proposes cost-of-pass to connect monetary cost with completion rate." / "MemoryOS reports the average number of LLM calls per response"
  where: p41-42 lines 1796-1797, 1826
- claim: No unified efficiency evaluation exists. Metrics are inconsistent and pipeline boundaries are unclear. The authors say multi-agent versus single-model role-play should be compared under matched budgets, which implies that comparison is rarely done now.
  number: none
  quote: "Unified efficiency evaluation is still missing for agents, as existing work reports inconsistent metrics and often collapses efficiency to token or API cost" / "Future work should compare these alternatives under matched resource budgets"
  where: p42-43 lines 1838-1864

LIMITS
- No original experiments. All performance and efficiency claims are secondhand and given without setup (no model, dataset, scale or baseline). I cannot tell you whether any quoted baseline is compute- or call-matched. The authors concede that matched-budget comparisons are missing from the field.
- The Introduction claims agents consume "exponentially more resources due to its recursive nature". This is unsupported, and the paper's own mechanism (the previous step's output becomes the next step's input) implies roughly quadratic growth in cumulative tokens. Avoid repeating "exponentially".
- The 0/1 indicator cost model has no call counts, no context-length term and no prefix-cache term. It is not usable for estimating real cost.
- It is not a survey of prompt caching or KV-prefix reuse in API serving. It covers latent KV memory only. Prompt caching, batching and model routing are mostly out of scope, apart from ToolOrchestra and BudgetMLAgent mentions.
- The pros and cons boxes are the authors' judgements, not findings.
- Dated: the arXiv v2 stamp is July 2026 and it cites 2026 arXiv papers (HyMem, SimpleMem, SkillRL and others). Many are single-paper claims I could not check.

BUILDS ON (credited for the framing and numbers; none verified by me beyond the survey text)
- Memory operations taxonomy: Du et al. [19], and Wang et al. [150] for agents versus LLMs.
- Cost-of-pass: Erol et al. [22] (Erol, El, Suzgun, Yuksekgonul, Zou).
- Numbers it relays: CoA [29] (Gao et al.) for the >30% figure, TinyAgent [21] (Erdogan et al.) for the prompt halving, LLMCompiler [61] (Kim et al.) for parallel calling gains (no figure given), LightMem [23], A-MEM [185], MemoryOS [59], OTC-PO [149] (Wang et al.), Budget-Aware tool use [88] (Liu et al.), TPS-Bench [181] (Xu et al.), CostBench [84] (Liu et al.), agentic plan caching [221] (Zhang, Wornow, Olukotun), and [144] for the 600-call figure.
- For primary-study numbers, go to those papers, not this survey.

CODE: none. The only formulas are the two cost expressions above (p6, lines 259-308).

FIGURES
- Figure 2 (p6): "From LLMs to agents: standalone reasoning to trajectory-level reasoning with memory, planning, and tool use, while introducing additional cost sources." It is the best candidate for the note, since it shows the extra cost terms at a glance. It is a small conceptual diagram. I did not open the image, so check it before using.
- Figure 1 (p4): timeline of the field. Skip it.
- Figure 3 (p7): memory lifecycle of construction, management and access. Useful as a levers map.
- Figure 4 (p26): tool-use taxonomy.
- Figure 5 (p35): planning overview.
- Table 5 (p40): benchmark and metric taxonomy, a useful checklist for "what to measure".

PROBLEMS
- Extraction hit a surrogate-character encoding error, which I worked around with UTF-8 replacement. A few words lost spaces ("onshared", "Memory-augmented reasoningprovides") and the Figure 1 text is jumbled. Nothing numeric was lost.
- No embedded instructions in the text.
- The PDF has no appendices.
- Figures were not opened visually. Captions came from the figures.py script (Figures 1-5).
- The cost-model line numbers refer to my /tmp extraction. Use page numbers for citing.
